q: Which amino acid has a nonpolar side chain?
h: Look for a side chain made only of carbon and hydrogen.
w: Valine's side chain is an isopropyl group, a hydrocarbon, so valine is nonpolar. Serine is polar neutral (O), lysine is basic (N) and aspartic acid is acidic.
x: Serine's side chain has an –OH group, and the polar O–H bond makes it a polar (hydrophilic) side chain.
Lysine's side chain ends in an amino group, which picks up H<sup>+</sup> to become charged. That makes lysine a basic amino acid, not a nonpolar one.
Aspartic acid's side chain has a –COOH group, which ionizes to –COO<sup>−</sup>. That makes it an acidic amino acid, not a nonpolar one.

q: At its isoelectric point (pI), an amino acid exists mainly as
c: a zwitterion with a net charge of zero
a cation with a net charge of +1
an anion with a net charge of −1
h: The pI is the pH where positive and negative charges balance.
w: At the pI the amino acid is H3N+–CHR–COO−, a zwitterion with zero net charge, so it does not move in an electric field.
x: A +1 cation is the main form at a pH well below the pI, where both the –COOH and the amino group carry H<sup>+</sup>.
A −1 anion is the main form at a pH well above the pI, where the amino group has lost its H<sup>+</sup>.
In water, amino acids are almost never present as neutral molecules with both –COOH and –NH<sub>2</sub>. The acid group gives its H<sup>+</sup> to the basic amino group.

q: Glycine (pI ≈ 6.0) is placed in a strongly acidic solution, at a pH far below its pI. Which form is present mainly?
h: At a pH far below the pI, extra H<sup>+</sup> is available. Which group picks it up?
w: Far below the pI the –COO− is protonated, giving H3N+CH2COOH with a net +1 charge. The zwitterion is the main form at the pI; H2NCH2COO− is the form far above the pI.
x: This is the zwitterion, the main form near the pI. Far below the pI there is plenty of H<sup>+</sup>, so ask which group would pick one up.
This form has lost the H<sup>+</sup> from the amino group. It is the main form far above the pI, in strongly basic solution.
Glycine is almost never present as this uncharged form in water. In strong acid, think about what extra H<sup>+</sup> does to each group.

q: A peptide bond is formed between
c: the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH<sub>2</sub> of the next
the side chains of two neighboring amino acids
the –NH<sub>2</sub> groups of two neighboring amino acids
the –COOH groups of two neighboring amino acids
h: A peptide bond is an amide bond, and water is released when it forms.
w: The carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next form an amide, –CO–NH–, releasing H2O. Side chains are not involved.
x: Side chains (R groups) are not part of the peptide bond. They hang off the backbone and stay free to interact with other groups.
Two amino groups cannot react to form an amide. An amide bond needs one acid group and one amine group.
Two carboxyl groups cannot form an amide. An amide bond needs one acid group and one amine group, with water released.

q: What is the name of the tripeptide Ala–Gly–Ser (written from the N-terminal end)?
h: Every residue except the C-terminal one gets the ending “-yl.”
w: Start at the N-terminus: alanyl, glycyl, then the C-terminal residue keeps its full name: alanylglycylserine. Reversing the order names a different peptide.
x: This names the residues starting from the C-terminal end. Peptide names start at the N-terminal residue, the one written first.
Here the last residue was also given the -yl ending. The C-terminal residue keeps its full amino acid name.
Peptide names change the ending of every residue except the last one to -yl. Simply stringing the full names together is not the naming rule.

q: How many peptide bonds are in a tetrapeptide?
h: Each bond connects two neighboring amino acids in a chain.
w: Four amino acids in a row are joined by 3 peptide bonds (n − 1).
x: That counts one bond per amino acid. A bond only forms between two neighbors, so the end residue does not need its own bond.
That is more bonds than there are amino acids. Each peptide bond links two neighboring residues; count the gaps between four beads on a string.
Two bonds would join only three amino acids, a tripeptide. Count the links needed to join four residues in a row.

q: In sickle-cell anemia, glutamic acid at position 6 of the hemoglobin β chain is replaced by valine. Which level of protein structure is changed directly?
h: Which level of structure is defined by the amino acid sequence?
w: Changing one amino acid changes the sequence, the primary structure. The new nonpolar valine then makes hemoglobin molecules clump, affecting higher levels as a consequence.
x: Secondary structure (α helix, β sheet) comes from backbone hydrogen bonds. A changed amino acid can affect it, but only as a consequence of something more basic.
The clumping of hemoglobin molecules is a downstream effect. Ask which level is defined directly by the order of amino acids.
The DNA mutation is the cause, but the protein made from it also changes: one amino acid is swapped for another in the chain.

q: The α helix and the β-pleated sheet are stabilized mainly by
c: hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups
disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains
salt bridges between acidic and basic side chains
h: Secondary structure involves only the repeating backbone atoms, not the R groups.
w: In secondary structure, the C=O of one peptide bond hydrogen bonds to the N–H of another. Disulfides and salt bridges involve side chains and belong to tertiary structure.
x: Disulfide bonds link cysteine side chains, which are R groups. They help hold the overall 3-D fold (tertiary structure), not the regular helix or sheet pattern.
Salt bridges form between charged R groups. They belong to tertiary structure; the helix and sheet come from repeating backbone atoms.
Peptide bonds join the backbone; they never link side chains. They hold the primary sequence together but do not create the helix or sheet shape.

q: A disulfide bond between two cysteine side chains in the same polypeptide chain stabilizes which level of protein structure?
h: Interactions between side chains that fold a single chain into its 3-D shape belong to which level?
w: Side-chain interactions within one chain (disulfides, salt bridges, H bonds, hydrophobic attractions) make up tertiary structure. Quaternary would require bonds between separate chains.
x: Primary structure is just the amino acid sequence held by peptide bonds. A disulfide is an extra link between side chains, not part of the sequence.
Secondary structure is the α helix and β sheet, held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups, not by side chains.
Quaternary structure involves interactions between separate polypeptide chains. Here both cysteines are in the same chain.

q: Hemoglobin is made of four polypeptide subunits (two α and two β) held together. This describes its
h: Which level applies only to proteins with more than one polypeptide chain?
w: The arrangement of multiple subunits in one active protein is quaternary structure. Each subunit has its own primary through tertiary structure.
x: Tertiary structure is the 3-D fold of a single polypeptide chain. Here we are describing how several chains fit together.
Secondary structure is the α helices and β sheets within a chain. It does not describe how separate subunits combine.
Primary structure is the amino acid sequence of one chain. It says nothing about how four chains are assembled.

q: A 70% isopropyl alcohol swab disinfects skin before an injection by denaturing bacterial proteins. Denaturation disrupts
c: secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, but not peptide bonds
only the peptide bonds that join the amino acids together
the primary structure, but no higher levels of structure
all levels, breaking the protein into free amino acids
h: Denaturation unfolds a protein. Does it break covalent peptide bonds?
w: Denaturing agents (heat, alcohol, acids, heavy-metal ions) break the interactions that fold the protein but leave the peptide bonds intact, so the primary structure survives. Breaking peptide bonds is hydrolysis.
x: Denaturing agents like alcohol unfold proteins; they do not break covalent peptide bonds. Breaking peptide bonds requires hydrolysis.
Primary structure is held by strong covalent peptide bonds, which survive denaturation. Unfolding affects the weaker interactions that fold the chain.
Breaking a protein into free amino acids is hydrolysis, as in digestion. An alcohol swab unfolds proteins but leaves the chain intact.

q: Which process breaks a protein's primary structure, as happens during digestion?
h: Primary structure is held together by covalent amide bonds. What reaction breaks an amide?
w: Digestive enzymes (or strong acid with heat) carry out hydrolysis, adding water across peptide bonds to free amino acids. Heat and pH changes only denature.
x: Heat denatures a protein by disrupting the interactions that fold it. The covalent bonds of the amino acid sequence stay intact.
Hydrogen bonds hold secondary and tertiary structure. Breaking them unfolds the protein but leaves the sequence of linked amino acids intact.
A small pH change can disrupt salt bridges and unfold a protein, but it does not break the covalent bonds of the primary structure.

q: In a globular protein dissolved in water, which side chain is most likely buried in the interior of the folded protein?
h: Polar and charged side chains like water. Where do nonpolar ones go?
w: Hydrophobic interactions pull nonpolar side chains such as leucine's isobutyl group into the interior, away from water. Charged lysine and glutamate and polar serine stay on the surface.
x: Lysine's side chain is positively charged, so it is attracted to water and stays on the protein surface.
Glutamate's side chain carries a negative charge, so it interacts well with water and stays on the protein surface.
Serine's –OH group hydrogen bonds with water, so this polar side chain tends to be on the surface, not hidden inside.

q: In phenylketonuria (PKU), the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine is missing. Which statement about a person with PKU is correct?
c: Tyrosine becomes essential, and phenylalanine intake must be limited
Phenylalanine becomes nonessential, so it can be eaten freely
Tyrosine builds up to toxic levels, so it must be avoided
Aspartame is safe because it contains no amino acids at all
h: If the conversion step is blocked, which amino acid piles up, and which one can no longer be made in the body?
w: Phenylalanine (and phenylpyruvate) builds up and can damage the developing brain, so its intake is limited. Because the body can no longer make tyrosine from phenylalanine, tyrosine must come from the diet. Aspartame contains phenylalanine, which is why diet drinks carry a PKU warning.
x: Phenylalanine is essential for everyone; PKU does not let the body make it. In PKU it actually builds up because it cannot be converted.
With the conversion step blocked, tyrosine is not made from phenylalanine. Think about which amino acid piles up and which one runs short.
Aspartame is a dipeptide made partly from phenylalanine. That is why diet drinks carry a warning for people with PKU.

q: Which amino acid is essential for adults and must be obtained from the diet?
h: Nonessential amino acids can be made in the body, often by transamination of keto acids from glycolysis or the citric acid cycle.
w: Lysine is essential (along with His, Ile, Leu, Met, Phe, Thr, Trp and Val, plus Arg, which this course counts as the conditionally essential tenth). Alanine, glutamate and serine are made from pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate and a glycolysis intermediate. Corn is low in lysine, so corn-based diets need complementary proteins.
x: Alanine is nonessential: the body makes it from pyruvate by transamination.
Glutamate is nonessential: the body makes it from α-ketoglutarate, a citric acid cycle intermediate.
Serine is nonessential: the body makes it from an intermediate of glycolysis.

q: Collagen’s three strands are held together partly by hydrogen bonds from hydroxyproline, a proline with an extra –OH group. Vitamin C is needed by the enzyme that adds that –OH. In scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), collagen is weak because
c: fewer –OH groups are added, so the strands form fewer hydrogen bonds
the peptide bonds between glycine and proline cannot form
the disulfide bonds holding the three strands together break
glucose units can no longer be attached to the strands
h: What attraction do –OH groups on neighboring strands form? What happens if fewer –OH groups are added?
w: Without vitamin C, proline is not converted to hydroxyproline, so there are fewer –OH groups and fewer hydrogen bonds holding the triple helix together. Collagen is weak, causing bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Peptide bonds still form normally.
x: Vitamin C is not needed to form peptide bonds; collagen chains are still built normally. The problem is a later change to proline.
Vitamin C's job here is adding –OH groups to proline, not making or keeping disulfide bonds. Think about what attraction those –OH groups form.
Attaching glucose is not the vitamin C-dependent step described here. Look again at what the enzyme adds to proline and what that group does.

q: Which protein is correctly matched with its function?
c: collagen: carries oxygen in the blood
h: Recall the protein classes: transport, storage, structural, hormone, enzyme, protection and contractile.
w: Myoglobin stores O2 in muscle. Hemoglobin (not collagen) transports O2, and collagen is structural. Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood glucose, antibodies (immunoglobulins) protect against infection, and actin and myosin contract muscle.
x: Collagen is a structural protein found in skin, tendons and bone. It does not carry oxygen.
Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood glucose. Starch is digested by enzymes such as amylase.
Antibodies (immunoglobulins) are protective proteins that fight infection. Muscle contraction uses contractile proteins such as actin and myosin.

q: A mixture of the three amino acids in the table undergoes electrophoresis in a buffer at pH 6.0. Compare the buffer pH with each pI. Which result is expected?
c: Lys moves to the − electrode, Asp to the + electrode, Gly stays
Lys moves to the + electrode, Asp to the − electrode, Gly stays
All three move to the − electrode, but at different speeds
Gly moves to the + electrode, while Lys and Asp stay in place
h: If pH < pI the amino acid is net positive; if pH > pI it is net negative; at pH = pI the net charge is zero.
w: At pH 6.0, lysine (pH below its pI) is net positive and moves to the negative electrode; aspartic acid (pH above its pI) is net negative and moves to the positive electrode; glycine is at its pI (zwitterion) and does not move.
x: This has the electrodes reversed. A net positive amino acid is attracted to the negative electrode, and a net negative one to the positive electrode.
Only amino acids with a net positive charge move toward the − electrode. Compare pH 6.0 with each pI: they are not all net positive.
Glycine's pI is 6.0, equal to the buffer pH, so its net charge is zero. Lys and Asp have pIs far from 6.0, so they carry a charge.

q: Which biomolecule is correctly matched with the linkage that joins its building blocks?
h: Think of the condensation reaction that builds each polymer and the functional group it forms.
w: Amino acids are joined by amide (peptide) bonds. Fats use ester bonds, polysaccharides use glycosidic (acetal) bonds, and nucleic acids use phosphodiester bonds in their backbone.
x: Triacylglycerols are made from glycerol and fatty acids, which form ester bonds, not ether bonds.
Polysaccharides are linked by glycosidic bonds between sugar units. Ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol in fats.
DNA nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone, not amide bonds.

q: Alanine, H<sub>2</sub>N–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–COOH, has a pI of 6.0. Which form is present mainly in a strongly basic solution, at a pH far above its pI?
h: At a pH well above the pI, OH<sup>−</sup> removes H<sup>+</sup>. Which groups lose a proton?
w: Far above the pI both acidic groups are deprotonated: –COOH → –COO− and –NH+3 → –NH2, giving H2N–CH(CH3)–COO− (net −1). The zwitterion is the main form at the pI, not far above it.
x: This is the zwitterion, the main form at the pI. Far above the pI, OH<sup>−</sup> removes another H<sup>+</sup>.
This fully protonated form (net +1) is found in strongly acidic solution, far below the pI.
This uncharged form is almost never present in water. In strongly basic solution, ask which groups lose H<sup>+</sup>.

q: Aspartic acid has the side chain –CH<sub>2</sub>COOH. What is its net charge in blood at physiological pH (7.4)?
h: At pH 7.4, every –COOH is ionized and the α-amino group is still –NH+3. Add up the charges.
w: At pH 7.4: α-COO− (−1), side-chain COO− (−1), α-NH+3 (+1). Net = −1, which is why Asp is called an acidic amino acid. Answering 0 forgets the ionized side chain.
x: A net charge of 0 forgets that the side-chain –COOH is also ionized at pH 7.4. Count all three charged groups.
A +1 charge would require extra positive groups. At pH 7.4 the carboxyl groups are negative and only the α-amino group is positive.
−2 counts both –COO<sup>−</sup> groups but forgets the α-amino group, which is still –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4.

q: A membrane protein has an α-helix that passes through the nonpolar interior of the lipid bilayer. Which side chains would most likely face the fatty acid tails?
h: “Like dissolves like”: which R groups are hydrocarbons with no charge or polar groups?
w: The lipid tails are nonpolar, so they contact nonpolar (hydrophobic) side chains such as Leu, Val and Ile. Basic, acidic and polar side chains prefer water and are found on surfaces exposed to the cytosol or the outside of the cell.
x: Lysine, arginine and histidine have basic side chains that can carry a positive charge. Charged groups avoid the nonpolar interior of the bilayer.
Aspartate and glutamate are negatively charged and serine is polar. These side chains prefer water, not fatty acid tails.
Serine, threonine and glutamine all have polar side chains (–OH or amide) that hydrogen bond with water, so they avoid the nonpolar lipid tails.

q: In a folded protein, which pair of side chains would most likely form a salt bridge?
h: A salt bridge is an ionic (electrostatic) attraction. Which pair carries opposite charges?
w: A salt bridge forms between a positively charged side chain (Lys) and a negatively charged one (Asp). Leu/Val form hydrophobic interactions, Ser/Thr form hydrogen bonds, and two Cys form a disulfide bond.
x: Leucine and valine have nonpolar hydrocarbon side chains with no charge. They attract each other by hydrophobic interactions.
Serine and threonine both have –OH groups, so they form hydrogen bonds. Neither is charged.
Two cysteine –SH groups form a covalent disulfide bond, not an ionic attraction.

q: Hemoglobin carries O<sub>2</sub> by binding it to the Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion in each heme group. Carbon monoxide poisoning is dangerous mainly because CO
c: binds the iron in hemoglobin more tightly than O<sub>2</sub> does
hydrolyzes the peptide bonds in hemoglobin's four chains
oxidizes the heme iron and converts hemoglobin into myoglobin
denatures plasma albumin so blood can no longer carry CO<sub>2</sub>
h: What happens if another molecule takes the O<sub>2</sub> spot on the iron and holds it tightly?
w: Hemoglobin in red blood cells transports O2 from the lungs to the tissues using Fe2+ in its heme groups. CO binds that iron far more tightly than O2, so less O2 is delivered. CO does not break peptide bonds.
x: CO does not break peptide bonds; that is hydrolysis. Think about what CO does at the iron where O<sub>2</sub> normally binds.
Hemoglobin cannot be converted into a different protein, myoglobin. Focus on how CO competes with O<sub>2</sub> at the heme iron.
CO's main danger involves hemoglobin and oxygen delivery, not albumin or CO<sub>2</sub>. Think about the Fe<sup>2+</sup> binding site.

q: Which amino acid side chain can form hydrogen bonds with water?
h: A hydrogen bond needs H bonded directly to F, O or N. Look for that in the side chain.
w: Serine has an O–H group in its side chain, so it can donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water (polar, hydrophilic). The other three side chains are only C and H, so they are nonpolar and hydrophobic.
x: Alanine's –CH<sub>3</sub> side chain has only C–H bonds, so it is nonpolar and cannot hydrogen bond with water.
Phenylalanine's side chain is a benzene ring plus CH<sub>2</sub>: only carbon and hydrogen, so it is nonpolar.
Valine's side chain is an isopropyl group made only of C and H, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.

q: Stomach acid (HCl, pH about 2) helps protein digestion. Which statement best describes how?
c: It denatures proteins, unfolding them so pepsin can reach the peptide bonds.
It hydrolyzes every peptide bond, releasing free amino acids.
It breaks the primary structure by oxidizing the side chains.
It converts proteins to glucose so they can be absorbed.
h: Low pH disrupts salt bridges and hydrogen bonds. Which levels of structure does that affect, and which bonds does pepsin hydrolyze?
w: HCl denatures proteins, disrupting secondary and tertiary structure so the chain unfolds and pepsin can hydrolyze the exposed peptide bonds. Acid alone does not break the primary structure into free amino acids; the enzymes do that.
x: Acid alone does not hydrolyze every peptide bond in the stomach. Breaking the chain into free amino acids is the job of digestive enzymes.
Stomach acid does not oxidize side chains, and the primary structure is held by covalent peptide bonds. Think about which weaker interactions low pH disrupts.
Proteins are digested to amino acids, not glucose. Think about what low pH does to a protein's folded shape.

q: The body makes nonessential amino acids by transferring an –NH<sub>2</sub> from glutamate to an α-keto acid. Why can't essential amino acids be made this way?
c: The body cannot make the α-keto acid carbon skeletons of essential amino acids.
There is not enough glutamate in cells to donate amino groups.
Essential amino acids contain no amino group.
Transamination works only in the stomach, not in cells.
h: Transamination needs two partners: an amino group donor and an α-keto acid acceptor. Which one is missing?
w: Transamination puts an –NH2 onto an α-keto acid. The body can make the keto acids (such as pyruvate → alanine) for nonessential amino acids but cannot synthesize the carbon skeletons of essential ones, so they must come from the diet. Amino groups (from glutamate) are not the limiting part.
x: Glutamate is not the limiting partner; amino groups are readily available. Ask which other partner in transamination the body cannot supply.
Every amino acid, essential or not, has an α-amino group. The issue is the rest of the molecule.
Transamination happens inside cells, mainly in the liver. The problem is a missing partner, not the location.

q: A free lysine molecule, side chain –(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>–NH<sub>2</sub>, is dissolved in blood plasma (pH 7.4). Adding up all its ionized groups gives what overall charge?
h: At pH 7.4, the α-carboxyl is –COO− and the α-amino is –NH+3. What happens to a basic side-chain amine?
w: –COO− (−1) + –NH+3 (+1) + side-chain –NH+3 (+1) = +1. Answering 0 forgets that the basic side chain is also protonated at physiological pH.
x: 0 forgets the side-chain amine. At pH 7.4 that basic –NH<sub>2</sub> picks up H<sup>+</sup> too, adding another positive charge.
A negative net charge would need more –COO<sup>−</sup> groups than –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> groups. Lysine has only one carboxyl group.
+2 counts both amino groups but forgets the α-carboxyl group, which is ionized as –COO<sup>−</sup> at pH 7.4.

q: Of these four amino acids, only one is classified as basic, with a side chain that is protonated (+) in body fluids. Which one?
h: Basic side chains contain an extra amine-type nitrogen that can accept H<sup>+</sup>. An amide nitrogen is not basic.
w: Arginine's side chain (a guanidino group) is protonated and positive at pH 7.4. Glutamine contains N, but in an amide, which is neutral; aspartic acid is acidic and negative.
x: Glutamine's side chain nitrogen is part of an amide, which is not basic. Its side chain stays neutral at pH 7.4.
Serine's side chain is –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. The –OH is polar but does not accept H<sup>+</sup>, so it is neutral.
Aspartic acid's side chain has a –COOH that loses H<sup>+</sup> to become –COO<sup>−</sup>, so it is acidic and negative, not basic.

q: In the tertiary structure of an enzyme, the side chain of leucine lies next to the side chain of isoleucine in the protein's interior. Which interaction holds them together?
h: Classify both side chains: are they polar, charged, sulfur-containing or nonpolar hydrocarbons?
w: Leucine and isoleucine both have nonpolar hydrocarbon side chains, so they cluster together away from water by hydrophobic interactions. Salt bridges need opposite charges, and disulfide bonds need two cysteines.
x: Salt bridges need opposite charges. Leucine and isoleucine side chains are uncharged hydrocarbons.
Disulfide bridges form only between two cysteine –SH groups. Leucine and isoleucine contain no sulfur.
Hydrogen bonds need H on O or N. Leucine and isoleucine side chains contain only C and H.

q: In the tetrapeptide Met–Lys–Trp–Glu, which amino acid is at the C-terminal end, with a free –COO<sup>−</sup> group?
h: Peptides are written from the N-terminus (free –NH+3) on the left to the C-terminus on the right.
w: By convention, the N-terminal amino acid is written first (Met) and the C-terminal amino acid last, so Glu has the free carboxylate group.
x: Met is written first, so it is the N-terminal residue with the free –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group.
Lys is in the middle of the chain, so both its backbone ends are tied up in peptide bonds.
Trp is an interior residue: its backbone amino and carboxyl groups are both used in peptide bonds.

q: A student links leucine, histidine and tyrosine into a three-residue chain, using each just once but in any order (for example, Leu–His–Tyr or Tyr–Leu–His). How many distinct sequences are possible?
h: Leu–His–Tyr and Tyr–His–Leu are different peptides because the N- and C-terminal ends differ. Count the possible orders.
w: There are 3 choices for the first position, 2 for the second and 1 for the last: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6. 27 (33) would allow repeats, which the problem does not.
x: 3 counts each amino acid once as a starting point but forgets the different ways to order the other two.
9 multiplies 3 × 3, as if two positions each had three choices. Once a residue is used it cannot be used again.
27 is 3 × 3 × 3, which allows the same amino acid to repeat. Here each one is used only once.

q: Mercury and lead poisoning damage many enzymes. Heavy-metal ions such as Hg<sup>2+</sup> and Pb<sup>2+</sup> denature proteins mainly by
c: binding to cysteine –SH groups and breaking disulfide bonds
hydrolyzing the peptide bonds that join the amino acids
adding water across the C=O groups of the peptide backbone
forming new hydrogen bonds that tighten the α helix
h: Denaturation changes shape (secondary and higher), not the amino acid sequence. Which side chain is especially attracted to heavy metals?
w: Heavy-metal ions bind strongly to sulfur in –SH groups and to carboxylates, breaking disulfide bonds and salt bridges so the protein unfolds. Denaturation leaves the peptide bonds (primary structure) intact.
x: Denaturation does not break peptide bonds; that is hydrolysis. Heavy metals change shape by binding to certain side chains.
Adding water across backbone groups would be a hydrolysis-type reaction, which heavy metals do not do. Think about which side chain atom metals attract.
Heavy metals unfold proteins rather than tightening them. Think about which side chain groups Hg<sup>2+</sup> and Pb<sup>2+</sup> bind.

q: Red blood cells carry oxygen bound to hemoglobin. How does one hemoglobin molecule bind O<sub>2</sub>?
c: Each of its four heme groups holds an Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion that binds one O<sub>2</sub>.
Its single polypeptide chain binds one O<sub>2</sub> at a time.
It stores O<sub>2</sub> in muscle tissue rather than carrying it in blood.
Its iron must be Fe<sup>3+</sup> to bind O<sub>2</sub>.
h: Hemoglobin has four subunits, each with one heme. What metal ion and charge are in the heme?
w: Hemoglobin has four subunits, each with a heme whose Fe2+ binds one O2, so one hemoglobin carries up to four O2. Storing O2 in muscle is the job of myoglobin; Fe3+ (methemoglobin) cannot bind O2.
x: Hemoglobin is not a single chain: it has four subunits (two α and two β), each able to bind O<sub>2</sub>.
Storing O<sub>2</sub> in muscle is myoglobin's job. Hemoglobin carries O<sub>2</sub> in red blood cells.
Iron in the Fe<sup>3+</sup> state (methemoglobin) cannot bind O<sub>2</sub>. The heme iron must be in the other oxidation state.

q: A biochemist treats a protein with a reducing agent that breaks all its disulfide bonds but no other bonds. Which level of structure is NOT changed?
c: the cross-links between cysteine side chains
h: For each level of structure, ask what holds it together. Which level would still be the same if every –S–S– link were cut?
w: Disulfide bridges link side chains and help hold the tertiary (and sometimes quaternary) structure. The sequence of amino acids, held by peptide bonds, is untouched: the primary structure stays the same.
x: Disulfide bonds help hold tertiary structure, so breaking them does change it. Look for the level held only by peptide bonds.
The folded 3-D shape depends partly on disulfide bonds, so breaking them changes it.
The cross-links between cysteine side chains are the disulfide bonds themselves, so the reducing agent removes them.

q: Corn protein is low in lysine, and bean protein is low in methionine. A vegetarian eats tortillas and beans at the same meal. Why is this a good choice?
c: Together they are complementary proteins supplying all essential amino acids.
Beans cause the body to synthesize the missing lysine from extra glucose.
Corn supplies nonessential amino acids, which then become essential ones.
Eating them together prevents the proteins from being hydrolyzed in digestion.
h: Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body. What happens when two foods are low in different essential amino acids?
w: Each food supplies the essential amino acid the other lacks, so together they are complementary proteins that provide all the essential amino acids. The body cannot make lysine (an essential amino acid) from glucose.
x: The body cannot make lysine from glucose; lysine is essential and must come from food.
Nonessential amino acids cannot be turned into essential ones. The body cannot make the carbon skeletons of essential amino acids.
Proteins are still hydrolyzed in digestion no matter how they are combined. The benefit is in which amino acids each food supplies.

q: Using the molar masses in the table, what is the molar mass of the tripeptide Gly–Gly–Gly?
h: Each peptide bond forms by condensation, releasing one H<sub>2</sub>O. How many peptide bonds are in a tripeptide?
w: A tripeptide has 2 peptide bonds, so 2 H2O are lost: 3(75.07) − 2(18.02) = 225.21 − 36.04 = 189.17 g mol⁻¹. 225.21 forgets the water lost; 207.19 removes only one water; 243.23 adds a water instead of removing them.
x: 225.21 is just 3 × 75.07. It forgets that a water molecule is lost each time a peptide bond forms.
207.19 removes only one water. A tripeptide has more than one peptide bond.
243.23 adds a water instead of subtracting. Forming peptide bonds is condensation, which releases water.

q: Which amino acid contains sulfur AND can form a disulfide bridge with another molecule of the same amino acid?
h: A disulfide bridge, –S–S–, forms when two thiol (–SH) groups are oxidized.
w: Cysteine has a –CH2SH side chain, and two –SH groups oxidize to –S–S–. Methionine also contains sulfur, but as a thioether (–S–CH3) with no –SH, so it cannot form disulfides.
x: Methionine contains sulfur, but as a thioether (–S–CH<sub>3</sub>) with no –SH group, so it cannot form a disulfide.
Serine's side chain is –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. It has oxygen, not sulfur.
Threonine's side chain has an –OH group and no sulfur.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain is –CH2OH. The –OH can hydrogen bond with water but carries no charge, so serine is polar neutral.
x: Nonpolar side chains contain only C and H. This side chain, –CH<sub>2</sub>OH, has an O–H group.
An acidic side chain has a –COO<sup>−</sup> group. This side chain has an –OH, which does not lose H<sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4.
A basic side chain has an extra amine nitrogen that carries a + charge. This side chain contains no nitrogen.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain ends in a carboxylate (–COO−), which is negatively charged at pH 7.4, so aspartate is acidic. The backbone COO− does not count; every amino acid has one.
x: A nonpolar side chain has only C and H. This side chain ends in a charged –COO<sup>−</sup> group.
Polar neutral side chains carry no charge. This side chain's –COO<sup>−</sup> is negatively charged at pH 7.4.
Basic side chains carry a + charge on nitrogen. This side chain ends in a negatively charged carboxylate.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain ends in an –NH+3 group, positively charged at pH 7.4, so lysine is basic. The backbone H3N+ is on every amino acid.
x: A nonpolar side chain has only C and H. This side chain ends in a charged –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group.
Polar neutral side chains carry no charge. This side chain's –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> is positively charged at pH 7.4.
Acidic side chains end in –COO<sup>−</sup>. This side chain ends in a positively charged nitrogen group; the backbone –COO<sup>−</sup> does not count.

q: Phenylalanine must be limited in the diet of people with PKU. How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain is a benzyl group (–CH2–C6H5) of only C and H, so phenylalanine is nonpolar and tends to be buried inside folded proteins.
x: Polar side chains contain O, N or S groups such as –OH or amides. This side chain is a –CH<sub>2</sub>– plus a benzene ring.
Acidic side chains have a –COO<sup>−</sup> group. This side chain has none; ignore the backbone carboxylate.
Basic side chains have an extra nitrogen that carries a + charge. This side chain has no nitrogen.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain ends in an amide (–CONH2). Amides are polar but neither acidic nor basic at pH 7.4, so glutamine is polar neutral. Students often confuse it with glutamate, whose –COO− side chain is acidic.
x: Nonpolar side chains contain only C and H. This side chain ends in a –CONH<sub>2</sub> group with polar C=O and N–H bonds.
This is not a –COO<sup>−</sup> group: the C=O carbon carries –NH<sub>2</sub>, making an amide. Amides do not lose H<sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4.
The nitrogen here is part of an amide (bonded to C=O), and amide nitrogens are not basic. It does not pick up H<sup>+</sup>.

q: Which amino acid has a nonpolar side chain?
h: A nonpolar side chain contains only carbon and hydrogen.
w: The correct structure is valine: its side chain is an isopropyl group, –CH(CH3)2, only C and H, so it is nonpolar. Serine (–CH2OH) is polar neutral, aspartate (–COO−) acidic and lysine (–NH+3) basic.
x: §B's side chain is –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. The –OH group makes it polar.
§C's side chain ends in –COO<sup>−</sup>, a negatively charged acidic group.
§D's side chain ends in –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, a positively charged basic group.

q: The dipeptide Ala–Gly is shown. The peptide bond joins which two labeled atoms?
h: A peptide bond is an amide bond: the carbonyl carbon of one amino acid bonded to the nitrogen of the next.
w: The peptide (amide) bond links the C=O carbon of alanine (b) to the N–H nitrogen of glycine (c). Atoms a and d are the α-carbons; the a–b and c–d bonds are ordinary C–C and N–C bonds inside each residue.
x: a and b are the α-carbon and carbonyl carbon of the same residue (alanine). That C–C bond is inside one amino acid.
c and d are the nitrogen and α-carbon of the same residue (glycine). That N–C bond is part of glycine itself.
a and d are the two α-carbons. They are not bonded directly to each other.

q: The –COOH group of glycine (first structure) reacts with the –NH<sub>2</sub> group of alanine (second structure), releasing H<sub>2</sub>O. Which product forms?
h: A peptide bond is an amide: C(=O)–NH. Glycine's carboxyl carbon bonds to alanine's nitrogen.
w: Condensation joins glycine's C=O carbon to alanine's N, giving the amide (peptide) bond of Gly–Ala; the free –NH2 stays on glycine and the free –COOH on alanine. The reversed dipeptide is Ala–Gly; the C(=O)–O–C(=O) structure is an anhydride, and the N–CH2 link has no C=O, so it is an amine, not an amide.
x: §B is the reversed dipeptide: alanine's C=O is bonded to glycine's N. That would come from alanine's –COOH reacting with glycine's –NH<sub>2</sub>.
§C joins two C=O groups through an O, a C(=O)–O–C(=O) anhydride link. A peptide bond needs a nitrogen.
§D links the two residues through N–CH<sub>2</sub> with no C=O next to the N. That is an amine, not an amide (peptide) bond.

q: Which structure shows alanine as it mainly exists in blood plasma (pH 7.4)?
h: At pH 7.4 the carboxyl group has lost H<sup>+</sup> and the amino group has gained H<sup>+</sup>.
w: At physiological pH alanine is a zwitterion: –NH+3 and –COO−, net charge 0. The uncharged form is not actually present in water; –NH+3/–COOH is the low-pH form, and –NH2/–COO− is the high-pH form.
x: §B is the uncharged form, with –NH<sub>2</sub> and –COOH. In water this form is almost never present.
§C has –COOH and –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, net +1. That is the main form at low pH, far below the pI.
§D has –NH<sub>2</sub> and –COO<sup>−</sup>, net −1. That is the main form at high pH, far above the pI.

q: Glycine is dissolved in stomach acid, at a pH far below its pI. Which structure is the main form present?
h: Far below the pI there is a lot of H<sup>+</sup>: every basic group is protonated and every acidic group keeps its H.
w: Far below the pI both groups carry H: –NH+3 and –COOH, net charge +1. The zwitterion (net 0) dominates at the pI (about 6), and –NH2/–COO− (net −1) far above the pI.
x: §B is the zwitterion (–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and –COO<sup>−</sup>), the main form near the pI. Far below the pI there is extra H<sup>+</sup> to pick up.
§C has –NH<sub>2</sub> and –COO<sup>−</sup>, net −1. That form is found far above the pI, in basic solution.
§D is the uncharged form, which is almost never present in water. In strong acid, think about what extra H<sup>+</sup> does.

q: Lysine is shown in its uncharged form. What is its net charge in a strongly acidic solution, at a pH far below its pI?
h: Far below the pI, protonate every amino group and leave the carboxyl group as –COOH.
w: Far below the pI both –NH2 groups (backbone and side chain) gain H+ to become –NH+3, and the –COOH stays neutral: net charge +2. Answering +1 forgets the side-chain amino group.
x: +1 protonates only the backbone amino group. Lysine also has a second amino group at the end of its side chain.
0 would be a zwitterion-type balance of charges. Far below the pI the carboxyl stays as –COOH, so it is not negative.
A negative charge needs an ionized –COO<sup>−</sup>, which happens at high pH. In strong acid the carboxyl keeps its H.

q: Aspartic acid is shown in its uncharged form. What is its net charge in a strongly basic solution, at a pH far above its pI?
h: Far above the pI every –COOH loses H+ and every –NH+3 loses H+ (becomes neutral –NH2).
w: Far above the pI both carboxyl groups become –COO− and the amino group is neutral –NH2: net charge −2. Answering −1 forgets the side-chain carboxyl.
x: −1 counts only one carboxylate. Aspartic acid has a second –COOH in its side chain.
0 balances one + and one − charge, as near the pI. Far above the pI the amino group is neutral –NH<sub>2</sub>.
A positive charge needs –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, which is lost at high pH. In strong base the groups lose H<sup>+</sup>.

q: Hair proteins (keratin) are held in shape by disulfide bridges, –S–S–. Which amino acid forms them?
h: A disulfide forms when two thiol (–SH) groups are oxidized and join.
w: The correct structure is cysteine: its side chain ends in a thiol, –SH. Oxidizing two cysteine –SH groups forms an –S–S– bridge (tertiary structure). Methionine has sulfur but as a thioether (–S–CH3) with no S–H; serine and threonine have –OH.
x: §B has sulfur, but as a thioether (–CH<sub>2</sub>–S–CH<sub>3</sub>) with no S–H bond. Without an –SH group it cannot form a disulfide.
§C's side chain is –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. It has an –OH group and no sulfur, so it cannot form –S–S– bridges.
§D's side chain is –CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>. It contains oxygen, not sulfur, so no disulfide is possible.

q: Four amino acids are drawn as they exist at pH 7.4. Which one is most likely found buried in the interior of a water-soluble, globular protein?
h: Ignore the common backbone. Look at each side chain: is it hydrocarbon only, or does it carry –OH, a charge, or N/O that attracts water?
w: Structure I is valine: its side chain, –CH(CH3)2, is pure hydrocarbon (nonpolar, hydrophobic), so it avoids water and is tucked inside the folded protein. II (threonine, –OH), III (glutamate, –COO−) and IV (arginine, charged guanidinium) are polar or charged and stay on the water-exposed surface.
x: II's side chain has an –OH group, which hydrogen bonds with water. Polar side chains tend to stay on the surface.
III's side chain ends in a negatively charged –COO<sup>−</sup> group. Charged groups attract water and stay on the protein surface.
IV's side chain carries a positively charged nitrogen group. Charged side chains prefer water and stay on the surface.

q: Four amino acids are drawn at pH 7.4. Which one can link to another copy of itself through a disulfide bond in a protein?
h: A disulfide bond forms when two –SH groups are oxidized. Two structures contain sulfur; only one has an –SH.
w: Structure II is cysteine, whose side chain ends in a thiol (–SH). Two cysteine –SH groups are oxidized to a –S–S– disulfide bridge, which stabilizes tertiary structure. Structure IV (methionine) also contains sulfur, but as a thioether (–S–CH3) that cannot form a disulfide; I (serine) and III (threonine) have –OH groups.
x: I's side chain is –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. It has oxygen but no sulfur, so it cannot form a disulfide.
III's side chain is –CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>, with an –OH and no sulfur. Disulfides need sulfur atoms.
IV contains sulfur, but as a thioether (C–S–CH<sub>3</sub>) with no S–H bond. A disulfide needs two –SH groups.

q: Glutamic acid has an acidic side chain, –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, in addition to its α-carboxyl and α-amino groups. What is its net charge at physiological pH (7.4)?
h: At pH 7.4 every –COOH loses H<sup>+</sup> (−1 each) and the –NH<sub>2</sub> gains H<sup>+</sup> (+1). Count both carboxyl groups.
w: At pH 7.4 both carboxyl groups are deprotonated to –COO− (−1 each) and the amino group is –NH+3 (+1): −1 − 1 + 1 = −1. “0” treats glutamic acid like a neutral amino acid and forgets the acidic side chain; −2 forgets the positive amino group.
x: 0 treats glutamic acid like a neutral amino acid. Its side-chain –COOH is also ionized at pH 7.4.
−2 counts both carboxylates but forgets the α-amino group, which is –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4.
A positive net charge would need more + groups than − groups. Glutamic acid has two carboxyl groups and only one amino group.

q: Glutamic acid (side chain –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH) has a pI of 3.2. One sample is placed in an electrophoresis buffer at a pH equal to its pI, and another in a buffer at physiological pH (7.4). How does it move in each?
c: At the pI it does not move; at pH 7.4 it moves toward the + electrode
At the pI it moves toward the − electrode; at pH 7.4 it does not move
It moves toward the + electrode in both of the two buffers
At the pI it does not move; at pH 7.4 it moves toward the − electrode
h: At pH = pI the net charge is zero. When the pH is above the pI, is the net charge positive or negative?
w: At its pI the amino acid has zero net charge, so it does not move. pH 7.4 is above the pI, so glutamate is net negative (two –COO− and one –NH+3, net −1) and moves toward the positive electrode.
x: At pH = pI the net charge is zero, so the amino acid does not move. And pH 7.4 is far from its pI of 3.2.
At the pI the net charge is zero, so there is no movement in that buffer.
The first part is right, but check the second. pH 7.4 is above the pI, so think about whether the net charge is positive or negative.

q: The dipeptide shown is drawn as it exists at pH 7.4. What is its name, written from the N-terminal end?
h: The N-terminus is the residue with the free –NH+3. Identify each side chain: –CH2OH is serine, –CH3 is alanine.
w: The residue with the free –NH+3 has a –CH2OH side chain: serine is the N-terminal residue. The residue with the free –COO− has a –CH3 side chain: alanine. Written N → C, the dipeptide is Ser–Ala. "Ala–Ser" reads the structure from the wrong end; threonine would need a –CH(OH)CH3 side chain.
x: This reads the dipeptide from the wrong end. Start with the residue that has the free –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group.
Threonine's side chain is –CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>. The residue drawn here has –CH<sub>2</sub>OH, with no extra methyl group.
Glycine's side chain is just H. The C-terminal residue here has a –CH<sub>3</sub> side chain on its α-carbon.

q: Which structure is a dipeptide, two amino acids joined by a peptide bond?
h: A peptide bond is an amide: the –COOH of one amino acid joined to the α-amino group of another. Check each structure for two α-carbons and an amide between them.
w: Structure I has two α-carbons (each with its own N) connected through a –C(=O)–NH– amide: it is the dipeptide Gly–Ala. II (asparagine) contains an amide, but in its side chain; it is a single amino acid. III joins glycine to serine through an ester (–C(=O)–O–), not a peptide bond. IV (lysine) has two amino groups but no amide at all.
x: II contains an amide, but it is in the side chain (–CH<sub>2</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>). There is only one α-carbon, so it is a single amino acid.
III joins two amino acid units through C(=O)–O, an ester link. A peptide bond needs C(=O)–NH.
IV is a single amino acid with an amino group on its side chain. It has two amino groups but no C(=O)–NH amide anywhere.

q: The table lists denaturing treatments and the interactions each one disrupts. Which level of protein structure survives every treatment in the table?
h: Which level is held together by covalent peptide bonds? None of the listed treatments is hydrolysis.
w: Every interaction in the table (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, salt bridges, disulfide bonds) is part of the secondary, tertiary or quaternary structure. None of the treatments breaks the peptide bonds, so the primary structure (the amino acid sequence) survives denaturation. Only hydrolysis (digestion) breaks primary structure.
x: Secondary structure is held by backbone hydrogen bonds, which are disrupted by treatments that break H bonds.
Tertiary structure depends on side-chain interactions like salt bridges, hydrophobic interactions and disulfides, which these treatments disrupt.
Quaternary structure is held by the same weak interactions between chains, so denaturing treatments disrupt it too.

q: Two regular folding patterns of a polypeptide backbone are compared in the table. Which identification is correct?
c: I = α-helix, II = β-pleated sheet; both are secondary structure
I = β-pleated sheet, II = α-helix; both are secondary structure
I = α-helix, II = β-pleated sheet; both are tertiary structure
h: The coil is the helix; the side-by-side strands are the sheet. Both are backbone hydrogen-bond patterns, so they belong to the same structural level.
w: A coiled spiral with hydrogen bonds along one chain is the α-helix (I); strands lying side by side held by hydrogen bonds between them form the β-pleated sheet (II). Both are stabilized by backbone C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds, so both are secondary structure. Tertiary structure involves side-chain interactions, not the backbone pattern.

head: Feature
I
II
rows: zig-zag strands lying side by side
within one chain, between C=O and N–H four residues apart

x: This swaps the two. The coiled spiral along one chain and the side-by-side strands are different patterns; match each to its name.
Tertiary structure comes from side-chain interactions. These patterns come from hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups.
Both patterns are held by the same kind of backbone hydrogen bonds, so they belong to the same structural level.

q: Lysine has a basic side chain, so its pI is high (about 9.7). At physiological pH (7.4), which is below its pI, what is lysine’s net charge?
h: Below the pI an amino acid carries extra H<sup>+</sup>. Which groups are charged at pH 7.4?
w: At pH 7.4 the α-carboxyl is –COO− (−1), the α-amino group is –NH+3 (+1), and the side-chain amino group is also protonated (+1): −1 + 1 + 1 = +1. Below its pI an amino acid is positive overall. “0” is the charge only at the pI; +2 forgets the negative carboxylate.
x: 0 is the net charge at the pI. At pH 7.4, below the pI, lysine carries extra H<sup>+</sup>.
A negative charge is expected above the pI. pH 7.4 is below lysine's pI.
+2 counts both amino groups but forgets the α-carboxyl, which is –COO<sup>−</sup> at pH 7.4.

q: Aspartic acid has a pI of about 2.8, glycine about 6.0, and lysine about 9.7. Which statement best explains the difference?
c: An extra acidic side chain lowers the pI; an extra basic side chain raises it
A larger side chain always gives a higher pI
Polar side chains lower the pI; nonpolar side chains raise it
The pI depends only on the number of carbon atoms in the side chain
h: Aspartic acid has an extra –COOH in its side chain; lysine has an extra –NH<sub>2</sub>. What does each do to the charge?
w: Aspartic acid’s side chain is acidic (–COOH), so it takes a lower pH to keep it neutral overall: a low pI. Lysine’s side chain is basic (–NH2), so it stays positive until the pH is high: a high pI. Glycine (R = H) sits in between. Size, polarity and carbon count don’t set the pI.
x: Size does not set the pI. Lysine and aspartic acid differ in the type of group on their side chains, not just in size.
Polarity alone does not set the pI; serine is polar but has a pI close to glycine's. What matters is whether the side chain gains or loses H<sup>+</sup>.
Carbon count does not set the pI. Look at which functional group is in each side chain and whether it is acidic or basic.

q: Curve 1 is the normal oxygen-binding curve of hemoglobin in blood at pH 7.4. Curve 2 was measured in blood from an actively exercising muscle, which contains more CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sup>+</sup> (a lower pH). What does the shift from curve 1 to curve 2 show?
c: At the lower pH, hemoglobin holds O<sub>2</sub> less tightly and releases more to the muscle
At the lower pH, hemoglobin holds O<sub>2</sub> more tightly and keeps it in the blood
At the lower pH, hemoglobin is fully denatured and can bind no O<sub>2</sub> at all
At the lower pH, hemoglobin binds O<sub>2</sub> exactly the same as at pH 7.4
h: At the same O<sub>2</sub> pressure, which curve shows less of the hemoglobin carrying O<sub>2</sub>?
w: Curve 2 lies to the right: at any O2 pressure hemoglobin is less saturated, so it holds O2 less tightly and unloads it more readily where CO2 and H+ are high (the Bohr effect), delivering O2 where it is needed. Curve 2 still reaches high saturation at high O2 pressure, so hemoglobin is not denatured.
x: A curve shifted to the right shows less saturation at each O<sub>2</sub> pressure, which means O<sub>2</sub> is held less tightly, not more.
Curve 2 still reaches high saturation at high O<sub>2</sub> pressure, so hemoglobin still binds O<sub>2</sub> and is not denatured.
The two curves are not the same; curve 2 is shifted. Compare their % saturation at the same O<sub>2</sub> pressure.

q: Use the oxygen-binding curve of hemoglobin. Blood leaves the lungs at an O<sub>2</sub> pressure of 100 mmHg and reaches resting tissue where the O<sub>2</sub> pressure is 40 mmHg. About what percentage of the hemoglobin's O<sub>2</sub>-binding sites unload their O<sub>2</sub> in the tissue?
h: Read the % saturation at 100 mmHg and at 40 mmHg from the curve. The difference is what was delivered.
w: From the curve, saturation is about 98% at 100 mmHg (lungs) and about 77% at 40 mmHg (tissue). The difference, roughly 98 − 77 ≈ 20%, is the fraction of sites that released O2. "75%" is the saturation remaining in the tissue, not the amount unloaded; the sigmoid shape means most of the O2 stays bound until the pressure falls further, as in exercising muscle.
x: About 75% is the saturation still remaining at 40 mmHg. The amount unloaded is the difference between the lung and tissue values.
About 98% is the saturation at 100 mmHg in the lungs. Subtract the tissue saturation to find how much was released.
50% would mean saturation drops to about half. Read the curve at 40 mmHg; it is still well above 50%.

q: Which of the structures drawn is an amino acid of the kind found in proteins?
h: A protein amino acid has an amino group AND a carboxylic acid group attached to the same (alpha) carbon.
w: Structure A is alanine: an –NH<sub>2</sub> and a –COOH are both bonded to the same carbon, the α carbon, which also carries the side chain –CH<sub>3</sub>. Lactic acid has –OH and –COOH (a hydroxy acid, no nitrogen); 2-aminoethanol has an amine and an alcohol but no carboxyl group; propanamide contains an amide group but no free amine or carboxylic acid.
x: §B has an –OH and a –COOH (a hydroxy acid) but no nitrogen, so it has no amino group.
§C has an amine and an alcohol, but no carboxylic acid group.
§D has a C=O bonded to –NH<sub>2</sub>, which is an amide. It has neither a free amino group nor a carboxylic acid.

q: Two side chains lie next to each other in the tertiary structure of an enzyme. For which pair is hydrogen bonding the main attraction holding them together?
h: Hydrogen bonds need an O–H or N–H plus an O or N. Charged pairs make salt bridges; hydrocarbon pairs are hydrophobic; two –SH groups make a disulfide.
w: Both serine and threonine side chains have an –OH, so one O–H can hydrogen-bond to the oxygen of the other: hydrogen bonding. Leucine/valine are hydrocarbons (hydrophobic interaction), lysine/glutamate carry opposite charges (salt bridge), and two cysteines are joined by a covalent disulfide bond.
x: Leucine and valine side chains are hydrocarbons with no O–H or N–H. They attract by hydrophobic interactions.
Lysine is positively charged and glutamate negatively charged, so their main attraction is an ionic salt bridge.
Two cysteine –SH groups are oxidized to a covalent disulfide bond, not held mainly by hydrogen bonds.

q: A chemist makes an alanine solution strongly basic with NaOH, to a pH far above its pI. Which of the structures drawn is the predominant form of alanine?
h: At high pH, OH− removes every acidic proton: the –COOH loses H+, and so does the –NH+3.
w: Far above the pI the carboxyl group is deprotonated (–COO−) and the base has also pulled the proton off the –NH+3, leaving a neutral –NH2: the anion H2N–CH(CH3)–COO−, net charge −1. The zwitterion is the main form at the pI and the cation far below it; the fully uncharged –NH2/–COOH molecule is not the major form at any pH.
x: §B is the zwitterion (–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and –COO<sup>−</sup>), the main form at the pI. In strong base OH<sup>−</sup> removes another H<sup>+</sup>.
§C has –COOH and –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, net +1. That is the main form in strong acid, far below the pI.
§D is the uncharged form, which is not the major form at any pH in water.

q: The tripeptide drawn (uncharged form) is completely hydrolyzed by digestive enzymes. What are the products?
c: Glycine, alanine and serine, using 2 H<sub>2</sub>O
Glycine, alanine and serine, using 3 H<sub>2</sub>O
One amino acid and one dipeptide, using 1 H<sub>2</sub>O
Three different carboxylic acids and NH<sub>3</sub>
h: Count the peptide (amide) bonds: each one hydrolyzed consumes one water and separates two amino acids.
w: A tripeptide has two peptide bonds, so complete hydrolysis uses 2 H2O and releases the three free amino acids: glycine (H side chain), alanine (–CH3) and serine (–CH2OH). "3 H2O" counts amino acids instead of bonds. Hydrolysis breaks only the amide bonds; the α-amino groups stay on their amino acids as NH+3, not as free NH3.
x: 3 H<sub>2</sub>O counts the amino acids instead of the peptide bonds. Each water breaks one peptide bond.
Complete hydrolysis breaks every peptide bond, not just one. Count how many amide bonds the tripeptide has.
Hydrolysis breaks only the peptide (amide) bonds. Each amino group stays attached to its own amino acid; none is released as NH<sub>3</sub>.

q: A water-soluble enzyme is placed in a nonpolar solvent such as hexane. Which change in its structure is most likely, and why does activity fall?
c: Hydrophobic side chains turn outward and polar ones inward, so the tertiary structure and active site are lost
The peptide bonds hydrolyze, so the primary structure and with it the active site are destroyed
New disulfide bonds form between all of the cysteine residues, locking the active site shut
The α-helices convert into β-sheets, but the shape of the active site itself is unchanged
h: In water, hydrophobic R groups hide inside and polar R groups face out. What happens when the solvent itself is nonpolar?
w: In hexane the driving force reverses: hydrophobic side chains are now happiest facing the solvent and polar side chains cluster inside, so the protein refolds or unfolds and the precisely shaped active site is lost: denaturation of tertiary structure. The covalent peptide bonds are not broken by a solvent (that needs hydrolysis), and disulfide formation requires an oxidizing agent.
x: A solvent like hexane does not hydrolyze peptide bonds; that needs water plus an enzyme or strong acid. The change here is to folding.
Disulfide bonds form only by oxidation of –SH groups, which a nonpolar solvent does not cause. Think about where nonpolar side chains would now prefer to be.
Any change in folding also changes the active site, whose shape depends on the folded protein. Think about which side chains now prefer to face outward.

q: Which amino acid is matched with BOTH its correct three-letter and one-letter abbreviations?
h: Some one-letter codes are simply the first letter, but when two amino acids share a first letter, one gets a different letter.
w: Glycine is Gly, G. Lysine is Lys, K (L is leucine). Glutamine is Gln, Q; Glu is glutamic acid. Tryptophan is Trp, W (T is threonine).
x: Lys is right, but L is the one-letter code for leucine. Lysine is K.
Glu is glutamic acid, whose one-letter code is E. Glutamine is Gln, Q.
Trp is right, but T is threonine. Tryptophan is W.

q: A tripeptide is written in one-letter code as M-A-C (N-terminal end first). How is it written with three-letter abbreviations?
h: M = methionine, A = alanine, C = cysteine.
w: M is methionine (Met), A is alanine (Ala), and C is cysteine (Cys): Met–Ala–Cys. The order stays the same, from the N-terminal to the C-terminal end.
x: Arg is arginine, whose one-letter code is R, not A.
Asn is asparagine, whose one-letter code is N, not A.
Lys is lysine (K). M stands for methionine.

q: Almost all of the amino acids in human proteins have the same configuration at the alpha carbon. Which one?
c: equal amounts of D and L (racemic)
none, because amino acids are not chiral
h: The D/L system for amino acids works like the one for sugars. Which form do human enzymes build proteins from?
w: Nearly all amino acids in human proteins are L-amino acids. D-amino acids occur mainly in some bacterial cell walls and certain antibiotics. Glycine is the one amino acid with no chiral carbon, so it is neither D nor L.
x: D-amino acids are rare in human proteins. Some bacteria and antibiotics contain them.
Enzymes are specific for one enantiomer, so cells do not build proteins from a racemic mixture.
Every common amino acid except glycine has a chiral alpha carbon (H, –NH<sub>2</sub>, –COOH and R are four different groups).

q: In a Fischer projection of an amino acid with –COO<sup>−</sup> at the top and the side chain at the bottom, where is the –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group in an L-amino acid?
h: In D/L notation, the group on the chiral carbon points right for D and left for L.
w: For amino acids, the –NH3+ group on the alpha carbon is drawn on the left in the L form and on the right in the D form, just as the –OH on the last chiral carbon of a sugar decides D or L.
x: On the right is the D form, which is rare in human proteins.
The top position holds the –COO<sup>−</sup> group in this Fischer projection.
The bottom position holds the side chain (R group).

q: Biuret reagent (blue Cu<sup>2+</sup>) turns violet when it reacts with two or more peptide bonds. Which sample gives a positive (violet) biuret test?
h: Which sample contains molecules with many peptide bonds?
w: The biuret test detects peptides and proteins with two or more peptide bonds. Egg albumin is a protein, so it turns violet. Free amino acids and sugars have no peptide bonds.
x: Glycine is a single amino acid with no peptide bonds, so the biuret reagent stays blue.
Glucose is a sugar and has no peptide bonds.
Alanine is a free amino acid with no peptide bonds, so the test is negative.

q: A student tests a solution of free alanine with ninhydrin and with biuret reagent. What results are expected?
c: ninhydrin turns purple; biuret stays blue
ninhydrin stays colorless; biuret turns violet
h: Ninhydrin needs a free amino group. Biuret needs two or more peptide bonds.
w: Ninhydrin reacts with the free –NH2 group of an α-amino acid to give a purple color, so it is positive. Alanine has no peptide bonds, so the biuret reagent stays blue: ninhydrin positive, biuret negative.
x: Biuret needs at least two peptide bonds. A single amino acid has none.
This is the pattern reversed. A free amino acid has a free amino group but no peptide bonds.
Ninhydrin reacts with the free amino group of an amino acid, so it is positive here.

q: Healthy kidneys keep proteins in the blood. A test on the urine of a patient with long-standing diabetes shows protein (proteinuria), a sign of kidney damage. A biuret test on this urine detects protein because the reagent reacts with
c: the peptide bonds of the protein
the urea that is always present in urine
the glucose spilled into the urine
h: What do all proteins contain that urea, glucose and fatty acids do not?
w: Biuret reagent forms a violet complex with peptide bonds (two or more in a row). Normal urine has only a trace of protein, so a positive result points to protein leaking through damaged kidneys.
x: Urea is always in urine but has no peptide bonds, so it does not give a positive biuret test.
Glucose in urine is detected by Benedict's test or a test strip, not by biuret.
Many molecules have –COOH groups. The biuret test needs peptide bonds.

q: A farmworker collapses on a very hot afternoon with a core body temperature above 40 °C (heat stroke). Rapid cooling is started at once. Why is cooling so urgent?
c: The longer proteins stay that hot, the more enzymes unfold and clump together, and many cannot fold back
Cooling re-forms peptide bonds broken by the heat
Cooling makes enzymes work faster than they do at 37 °C
Heat converts proteins into fats, and cooling reverses this
h: Heat breaks the weak attractions that hold a protein's shape. What happens to an unfolded enzyme's activity?
w: High temperature breaks the hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and hydrophobic interactions that hold an enzyme's shape, so enzymes denature and can clump (aggregate). Peptide bonds survive, but many unfolded proteins do not refold, so every minute counts.
x: Denaturation by heat does not break peptide bonds. The primary structure stays intact; the folded shape is lost.
Enzymes have their highest activity near 37 °C. Cooling a patient back toward normal does not make enzymes faster than normal.
Heat changes a protein's shape. It does not turn protein into fat.

q: Nitrate from fertilizer and manure can seep into Valley well water. In the body some nitrate becomes nitrite, which converts the Fe<sup>2+</sup> in hemoglobin's heme to Fe<sup>3+</sup>, forming methemoglobin, which cannot carry O<sub>2</sub>. What has happened to the iron?
c: It has been oxidized: it lost an electron
It has been reduced: it gained an electron
It has been hydrolyzed by water
It has been removed from the heme
h: Going from Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup>, did the iron gain or lose a negative electron?
w: Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e−: the iron lost an electron, so it was oxidized. Nitrite is the oxidizing agent. Fe3+ heme cannot bind O2, so less oxygen is delivered, which can make an infant's skin look bluish.
x: Gaining an electron would lower the charge, for example Fe<sup>3+</sup> to Fe<sup>2+</sup>. Here the charge rises.
Hydrolysis breaks a bond by adding water. A change in the charge of iron is a redox change.
The iron stays in the heme. Only its charge changes, which is why it can no longer carry O<sub>2</sub>.
